title: Eight-Way Path Across a Grid
statement:
You get an n × n grid of 0 (open) and 1 (blocked). Walk from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell, stepping only on open cells. From a cell you may step to any of its eight neighbours: up, down, left, right or diagonal.

Return the number of cells on the shortest such path, counting both the start and the end cell. Return -1 if there is no path, including when the start or end cell is blocked.

examples.why: One diagonal step. The path has two cells.
(0,0) → (0,1) → (1,2) → (2,2). The diagonal step saves a cell over going around the corner.
The start is blocked, so there is no path at all.

hints: "Shortest" with every step costing the same is a hint. Which search finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs?
BFS from the top-left cell. Each cell's distance is fixed the first time you reach it. Remember to check eight directions, not four.
Mark a cell visited when you push it into the queue, not when you pop it, or the same cell enters the queue many times. Handle a blocked start or end before starting.

explain.intuition:
Every step costs one cell, so this is a shortest path in an unweighted graph: the cells are nodes and each open cell connects to its up to eight open neighbours. BFS explores in rings of equal distance, so the first time it reaches a cell, it has used the fewest steps possible.

Two details matter. Count cells, not moves, so the start has distance 1. And mark cells as seen at the moment you add them to the queue; otherwise a cell can be added once by each of its eight neighbours.
steps: Push (0, 0) with distance 1 and mark it (for example set it to 1 in a copy of the grid).
Pop cells in order. If the cell is the bottom-right corner, return its distance.
Otherwise, for each of the eight neighbours that is inside the grid and open, mark it and push it with distance + 1.
pitfalls: Using only four directions. The second example then needs 5 cells instead of 4.
Counting moves instead of cells: a 1×1 open grid has answer 1, not 0.
Forgetting to check that the start cell itself is open.

solutions.title: Relax distances until nothing changes
solutions.idea: Start with distance 1 at the start cell. Sweep the grid repeatedly, improving each open cell from its neighbours, until a sweep changes nothing.

solutions.title: Breadth-first search
solutions.idea: BFS from the top-left cell over open cells with eight directions. The first time the bottom-right cell is popped, its distance is the answer.

followups: Diagonal steps now cost more than straight ones. Which algorithm replaces BFS?
Return the path itself, not only its length. What extra information do you store per cell?
